To jaunce means to prance — to move with a lively, bouncing, high-stepping energy. Think of the way a spirited horse lifts its legs with flair and bounces forward, or the way a person might strut about with a spring in their step. That quality of energetic, rhythmic, somewhat showy movement is what "jaunce" captures.

But the word carries a second, closely related shade of meaning: to ride hard, jolting and exhausting something or someone. This is really just the darker side of the same image. A horse prancing under a relentless rider isn't just moving lightly and freely — it's also being spurred, shaken, and worn down. So "jauncing" can describe either the lively movement itself, or the act of pushing and jolting something along until it's tired out.
The two senses laid out clearly

• Sense 1 — To prance or frolic: Moving in a bouncy, spirited, energetic way. Lively, a little showy.
  • Sense 2 — To ride hard and jolt: To exhaustingly drive or shake something (often a horse, or by metaphor, a person) through vigorous, relentless movement.

These two senses are really two sides of one coin: the same bouncing, jolting motion — only in Sense 1 you're watching it with admiration, and in Sense 2 you're feeling the bruising effect of it.
The word in real use — Shakespeare

The earliest known use of "jaunce" as a verb traces back to the late 1500s, and our earliest solid evidence for it comes from William Shakespeare. He used it in two of his plays, and these real examples are the clearest possible way to see the word in action.

In Act II, Scene V, the Nurse returns from a long, tiring errand and collapses with exhaustion, crying: "Fie, how my bones ache! What a jaunce have I had!" and "Beshrew your heart for sending me about / To catch my death with jauncing up and down."

Here "jauncing up and down" means running frantically back and forth — being jolted and worn out by all that rushing around. The Nurse is not prancing prettily; she is exhausted by the endless bouncing, hurrying movement Juliet's errand forced on her. This is Sense 2 — the tiring, jolting side of the word.

In Act V, Scene V, the deposed King Richard compares himself bitterly to a horse being ridden by his usurper, saying: "I was not made a horse, and yet I bear a burden like an ass, / Spurred, galled, and tired by jauncing Bolingbroke."

This is one of Shakespeare's most powerful uses of the word. Richard is saying that Bolingbroke (who took his throne) is riding him — spurring him, wounding him (galling him), wearing him out — just as a rough rider jaunces a horse. "Jauncing Bolingbroke" means Bolingbroke, who prances and rides hard, who pushes and exhausts those beneath him. Both senses of the word flicker here at once: Bolingbroke moves with the energy and swagger of Sense 1, while Richard suffers the bruising exhaustion of Sense 2.

"Jaunce" is classified as archaic — meaning it belongs to an older form of the English language and is no longer part of everyday speech. The term occupies one of the lowest positions among commonly used words in the English dictionary. You will not hear it in conversation today. You are most likely to encounter it when reading older literature, especially Shakespeare, or in historical texts from the 16th and 17th centuries.

The word sits in a family of similarly-feeling words: think of "jaunt" (a short lively trip), "jaunty" (having a bouncy, cheerful confidence), and even "bounce" (which may have influenced "jaunce" itself). All of them share that same quality of energetic, springy movement. "Jaunce" is simply the verb that captures that energy in its most physical, horse-and-rider form — either the lively prancing of it, or the wearing, jolting exhaustion of being on the receiving end.
